newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Protesters back off from APEC confrontation.
newsitem.headline: Protesters back off from APEC confrontation.

text.p: Thousands of leftists on Monday retreated from a confrontation with riot police and called off a planned protest cavalcade to the APEC summit venue at Subic Bay, saying it would be "suicide".

Hours before U.S. President Bill Clinton and other world leaders gathered for their summit, police blocked the highway leading to the venue with cargo trucks and fire engines and a police chief said his men were determined to stop the convoy.

"Considering the large number of our enemy, we will not sacrifice our bodies, we will not sacrifice our force because that will be suicide," leftist leader Nathaniel Santiago told protesters assembled at Dinalupihan town, about 20 km (12 miles) from Olongapo city where the summit venue is located.
"We will no longer continue," chief rally organiser Satur Ocampo told reporters.
"We are realistic enough to recognise that we cannot break through this last barricade," he added, referring to columns of police and the trucks blocking the protesters' path.
Opponents of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum say developing countries are not ready for the rigours of free trade that APEC advocates and fear rising unemployment.
Most of the estimated 7,000 protesters drove into Dinalupihan in convoy, braving heat and rain, enduring hunger and defying numerous police blocks that slowed down the cavalcade.
Many rode in distinctive "jeepneys" -- colourful minibuses modelled on World War Two jeeps -- flying streamers with slogans slamming APEC.
Regional police chief General Edgardo Aglipay told reporters he had about 2,000 police ready to stop the cavalcade and added: "It's up to them if they kill us."

He said Olongapo residents supporting APEC were also ready to block the protesters. Reporters saw dozens of pro-APEC residents guarding the boundary between Olongapo and Dinalupihan, checking the identity papers of people entering the town. Some of the residents carried wooden clubs.

Philippine Communist Party founder Jose Maria Sison denounced the "repressive actions" taken by police against the APEC protesters and warned that the communist-led National Democratic Front (NDF) might withdraw from current peace talks with Manila.
Sison, who lives in exile in the Netherlands, also demanded the release of NDF officer Danilo Borjal, who was arrested by security forces last week.

"Should (the government) violently suppress or disrupt the anti-APEC protest actions, the broad masses of the people have all the reason to expand and intensify their resistance," Sison said in a statement faxed to news organisations from his exile home.
"Consequently, the NDF will have to consider withdrawing from peace negotiations," he said.

The cavalcade, made up of three separate caravans, left Manila on Sunday for the 80-km (50 mile) drive to Subic Bay but was slowed down by police checkpoints before it reached Dinalupihan, where protesters spent the night.
The protesters included more than 100 foreigners who held up "Junk APEC" streamers and chanted anti-APEC slogans.

The caravans created huge traffic jams and stranded thousands of commuters, many of whom abandoned their cars on roadsides and walked to their destinations, carrying their belongings with them and tugging their children along.

Stranded businessman Loi Federico told leftist leader Ocampo at a roadside meeting: "I am just an ordinary motorist and I have with me my wife and my five children. We have been hiking for seven hours...I don't believe in your cause."
Unable to break the police barricade at Dinalupihan, the protesters staged a rally in front of the town hall, lambasting the APEC summit and singing Christmas carols.
